RESULTS: The immediate postoperative course was unremarkable with control of intraocular pressure without additional glaucoma medications. At first follow-up, 2 weeks post surgery, conjunctival dehiscence with partial extrusion and exposure of the reticulated hyaluronic acid implant was observed. Under topical tobramycin ointment a gradual limbal readaptation of the conjunctiva over the surface of the exposed parts of the implant with formation of a filtration bleb was noted. Therefore, surgical revision remained unnecessary. CONCLUSIONS: Implant exposure following nonpenetrating antiglaucomatous surgery is a specific complication, which can appear whenever intrascleral implants are used. Depending on the local situation nonsurgical treatment may be successful.

Title: Pilot study of glaucoma drainage implant surgery supplemented with reticulated hyaluronic acid gel in severe glaucoma.

Journal/Date: European journal of ophthalmology (2015)

--- ABSTRACT ---
[PURPOSE]: This pilot study, the first of its type, was conducted to determine the clinical outcome of glaucoma drainage implant (GDI) surgery supplemented with injectable crosslinked hyaluronic acid (HA) in patients with severe glaucoma.
[METHODS]: This was a retrospective chart study involving 10 eyes of 10 patients with severe glaucoma (glaucomatous visual field loss worse than -20 dB) who had previously undergone GDI surgery supplemented with crosslinked HA with a 2-year follow-up. Surgical success was defined as intraocular pressure (IOP) <21 mm Hg with a reduction of ≥40% (definition A) or ≥50% (definition B) from baseline IOP on 2 consecutive follow-up visits, IOP >5 mm Hg on 2 consecutive follow-up visits, and neither reoperation of glaucoma nor loss of light perception vision.
[RESULTS]: The mean ± SD baseline IOP before GDI was 38.5 ± 10.7 mm Hg, and the mean IOP at the last follow-up visit was 13.0 ± 5.0 mm Hg, with a mean pressure drop of 24.4 ± 10.9 mm Hg (62%; p = 0.005). According to definition A, life-table analysis showed an overall success rate of 80%, while according to definition B, the success rate was 50% after 24 months of follow-up. Complications were infrequent and not serious. No complications resulting from the reticulated HA therapy itself were observed.
[CONCLUSIONS]: In eyes with severe glaucoma, the intraoperative application of crosslinked sodium HA gel may improve the efficacy of GDI surgery.

key_findings.finding: Direct human evidence exists but is limited to one small retrospective pilot: 10 eyes with severe glaucoma (visual field worse than −20 dB) underwent glaucoma drainage implant surgery supplemented with injectable crosslinked/reticulated hyaluronic acid gel and were followed for 2 years. Mean IOP fell from 38.5±10.7 to 13.0±5.0 mmHg (62% reduction; p=0.005); success was 80% using a ≥40% reduction definition and 50% using a ≥50% definition. Complications were infrequent/not serious, and no complication was attributed specifically to the HA gel. This supports feasibility, not comparative efficacy, because the study was retrospective, uncontrolled, and only 10 eyes.

The intervention is described as injectable crosslinked sodium hyaluronate / reticulated hyaluronic acid gel; Healaflow/HealaFlow (Anteis) is the key product synonym identified in related glaucoma literature. However, the direct pilot abstract does not provide enough detail to verify the exact commercial formulation, dose, placement protocol, or whether every case used Healaflow specifically; these should be confirmed before protocol development.

source_tools.relevance: HealaFlow identified as high-molecular-weight cross-linked hyaluronic-acid gel in human glaucoma surgery

key_findings.finding: Indirect human evidence supports biologic plausibility but is not evidence for tube shunts. In deep sclerectomy, 55 eyes treated with crosslinked sodium hyaluronate (HEALAflow) had mean IOP reduction from 21.6 to 11.5 mmHg and medication reduction from 2.4 to 0.5; 5 eyes had hypotony (<6 mmHg) and 3 had iris incarceration. In a prospective 60-eye trabeculectomy comparison, HealaFlow and low-dose MMC produced similar 12-month IOP reduction and similar complications, with no clear superiority of HealaFlow. These studies involve nonpenetrating surgery/trabeculectomy, not Ahmed, Baerveldt, Molteno, or other plate/tube drainage implants.

source_tools.relevance: Prospective HealaFlow versus MMC trabeculectomy outcomes

key_findings.finding: Indirect trabeculectomy evidence suggests HealaFlow may be safe but does not reliably improve outcomes over surgery alone: a 40-eye retrospective case-control study found final IOP 14.9±3.2 versus 14.8±3.3 mmHg and medication burden 0.6±0.8 versus 0.55±0.9 at 6 months for HealaFlow versus control, with no significant between-group advantage. Therefore, any claim that HA reduces fibrosis/encapsulation or medication burden after a tube implant remains unproven.

source_tools.relevance: Human comparative IOP and medication data

key_findings.finding: The literature search identified no additional human study directly combining a glaucoma drainage device/tube shunt with crosslinked HA gel beyond the 10-eye pilot; older HA implant studies mainly concern nonpenetrating surgery. Historical Molteno literature mentions intracameral hyaluronic acid (Healon) as an operative technique to reduce early hypotony/shallowing, but that is transient viscoelastic use inside the anterior chamber, not peri-plate or subconjunctival reticulated/crosslinked HA gel supplementation and should not be treated as equivalent evidence.

source_tools.relevance: Search results identifying the single direct GDI+HA pilot and older nonpenetrating studies

key_findings.finding: There are clinically relevant safety gaps for translation to severe-glaucoma tube surgery: the direct study is too small and uncontrolled to characterize uncommon events or compare hypotony, tube occlusion, infection, inflammation, encapsulation, fibrosis, reoperation, corneal decompensation, or long-term gel persistence. HA implant literature also reports implant exposure/extrusion after nonpenetrating surgery, while standard Ahmed surgery can have early hypotony despite viscoelastic fill. These gaps justify a carefully monitored pilot, but not routine adoption or claims of superiority.

source_tools.relevance: Direct pilot limitations and absence of gel-attributed complications
Tube-surgery viscoelastic safety signal for hypotony

key_findings.finding: Overall judgment: a pilot clinical study is scientifically justified as a feasibility/safety study in carefully selected severe glaucoma patients, because there is direct precedent for the exact concept and a large unmet need, but the evidence is insufficient for an efficacy trial or routine clinical use. The pilot should prospectively define the exact HA product and placement, include a contemporaneous tube-only comparator if feasible, and measure IOP, medication burden, hypotony, inflammation, tube/plate complications, encapsulation or bleb morphology, reoperation, and visual outcomes for at least 24 months; regulatory/device-use review is essential because the gel’s use as an adjunct around a tube implant may not match its cleared/approved indication.
